title: Card Chargebacks: A Record Trail for Direct Villa Bookings
metaDescription: Track disputed villa booking payments with a clear case register, settlement trail and illustrative IDR example. Avoid counting refunds and chargebacks twice.
excerpt: A practical record-keeping workflow for direct-booking card disputes: connect the original booking, payment, settlement, case status and final cash movements.
imageAlt: Illustrative Bali accounting workspace used to explain booking payment and dispute records
contentHtml:
Keep a disputed payment connected to the original booking

A chargeback creates another record to reconcile. Keep the original booking, the guest payment, the processor settlement, the disputed amount, any separately documented fees and the eventual decision linked together. For a Bali villa owner, this trail explains why cash changed without deleting the history of the stay. It also helps prevent an ordinary refund and a disputed payment from being counted twice. This guide describes a record-keeping workflow; the accounting and tax treatment still depends on the actual facts and professional review.

Who this applies to

This guide is for villa owners and managers who accept direct-booking card payments and need to explain a disputed payment in their monthly records. It also helps a remote owner review a manager's statement when a later settlement is lower than expected. The process is useful for one property or several, provided each case remains assigned to the correct property and operating entity.

Payment providers have different processes and availability. Check the provider and account actually used by the business. A description of one provider is not a promise that its service is available for your entity, and this article does not recommend a provider or give instructions for winning a dispute.

For context, Stripe describes a card dispute as a payment contested through the account holder's bank. Its documentation distinguishes the disputed amount, provider fees and the subsequent decision. Those are useful distinctions for a records schedule. They do not establish the fees, deadlines or outcome for your particular booking.

Start with a case register

Create one case reference and connect it to the booking reference and payment reference. The case reference should stay the same when a provider sends another notification. Avoid treating every email or dashboard status change as a new transaction. A single contested payment can produce several messages and balance movements over time.

Keep the booking dates separate from the payment date, original settlement date and dispute date. A stay in September can produce a dispute in October and a decision in a later reporting period. Removing the original payment from September because the case opened in October destroys the trail the owner needs to understand both periods.

RecordWhat to retainWhat it helps explain
BookingBooking ID, property and stay datesWhich operating activity the payment relates to
PaymentPayment ID, currency, amount and payment dateWhat the guest originally paid
SettlementSettlement ID, deductions and matching bank receiptHow the payment reached the accounts
DisputeCase ID, disputed amount, status and dated noticesWhy a later balance movement happened
DecisionFinal notification and any resulting movementWhether the case and its money trail can be closed

Store supporting documents through the business's agreed secure process. The working register needs a reference to the evidence, not unnecessary guest identity documents or payment-card details. Keep access appropriate to the people responsible for the case and the financial review.

Separate the movements before explaining the outcome

The disputed amount and the provider's fee are separate items. The amount contested can differ from the original booking total. A provider may also settle several bookings together or deduct an adjustment from a later payout. Work from the transaction-level statement and its settlement reference rather than guessing from the size of a bank deposit.

First identify the original payment and settlement. Then identify the later adjustment and any fee that the statement separately documents. Finally, match the provider's decision to any money returned. A case marked resolved does not by itself prove that the expected return has reached the bank or appeared in a later settlement.

If the adjustment was netted against another payout, show the bridge from the underlying transactions to that payout. Do not create a separate bank debit that never happened. If a statement is missing, leave the movement unresolved and record who will obtain the evidence. A question register is more useful than an unexplained balancing figure.

An illustrative IDR cash-movement example

The following example is fictional. It assumes the statements confirm three separate bank movements so the arithmetic is easy to follow. The amounts are not a quote for any provider's fees, a client result, a complete set of accounts or a tax calculation. In a real case, deductions might instead be included in later settlements.

A guest originally pays IDR 12,000,000. A hypothetical processing charge of IDR 300,000 is withheld, and the bank receives IDR 11,700,000. Later, an IDR 4,000,000 portion is disputed. For this example only, the records show a further bank debit of IDR 4,150,000, comprising the disputed amount and a separately documented hypothetical case fee of IDR 150,000.

Documented movementCash movement in this exampleCumulative net movement
Original settlement after processing chargeIDR 11,700,000 receivedIDR 11,700,000
Disputed amount and hypothetical case feeIDR 4,150,000 paid outIDR 7,550,000
If the disputed amount is subsequently returnedIDR 4,000,000 receivedIDR 11,550,000

The final row assumes the hypothetical case fee is not returned. Confirm actual fee handling from the provider's statement. If the disputed amount is not returned, the documented net movement in this example remains IDR 7,550,000. If the case is still open, show that status without presenting a potential future recovery as money already received.

These figures describe the selected cash movements only. They do not determine revenue, profit, a receivable, an expense classification or the period in which an accounting adjustment belongs. Give the underlying booking, contract and provider evidence to the person responsible for those judgments. An owner statement should make the uncertainty visible.

Check for a refund before recording another reduction

Look for an earlier refund linked to the same payment. A guest complaint, a refund and a formal dispute are different events, but they can concern the same booking. Search by payment reference and booking reference rather than relying only on the guest name or a similar amount.

If a refund already appears in the records, retain its confirmation, amount, currency and settlement date. Put it beside the disputed amount and the provider's case explanation. Ask the responsible case handler to explain the relationship. Do not assume that the earlier refund has automatically closed the dispute, and do not record a second voluntary refund simply because another notice arrived.

A bookkeeper can document the differences and make the financial trail reviewable. The authorised person handling the dispute decides what response is appropriate using the actual provider's requirements. Keep those responsibilities clear so a record-keeping exercise does not accidentally become an instruction to move money.

Show the case clearly in the owner report

Use a small exception section with the booking reference, property, amount under review, last confirmed status and next responsible person. Explain whether the movement affected a bank account, a provider balance or a later settlement. Keep this explanation separate from ordinary booking activity so the owner can follow the change.

Carry an open case forward with its original reference. Add new evidence and dated status changes rather than overwriting the previous month's note. When the provider announces a decision, check the financial movement separately before closing the reconciliation item. If the money has not yet appeared, the reporting question remains open even if the case status has changed.

For wider context, review our direct-booking payment processor reconciliation guide and the process for investigating unmatched villa bank transactions. The same discipline applies: identify the source, connect the movement and preserve the unresolved question.

What owners get wrong

Deleting the original booking payment

This makes the original settlement harder to explain and obscures the later dispute. Preserve the original evidence and add the new case and movements. Have the appropriate reviewer determine any accounting adjustment.

Calling every later deduction a refund

A provider deduction can contain a disputed amount, a fee or another adjustment. Retain the provider's labels and transaction references before deciding how the items should be presented in the books.

Closing the record when a notification arrives

A notification and a financial settlement are separate evidence. Match the status to the actual transaction and bank or payout record. Keep a follow-up item if the expected movement has not been confirmed.

A repeatable month-end checklist

  1. List open cases by property, booking and payment reference.
  2. Attach the original booking, payment and settlement evidence.
  3. Identify the disputed amount and separately documented fees.
  4. Check whether an ordinary refund was already recorded.
  5. Match each movement to the provider statement and actual bank or settlement record.
  6. Separate money already received from a possible future recovery.
  7. Record the current case status, unresolved question and responsible person.
  8. Retain the previous reporting notes and add dated updates.
  9. Ask the responsible adviser to review accounting or tax judgments.
  10. Close the reconciliation item only when the evidence explains the final position.

The useful deliverable is an understandable case trail. It should allow the owner, manager and reviewer to connect the original payment to the eventual position without relying on memory. If the same gaps recur, improve the document handover and case register before adding more spreadsheet adjustments.

Frequently asked questions

Is a chargeback the same as a refund?

No. A refund is a different event from a payment disputed through a bank or payment system. Keep the references and statements for each and check whether they concern the same original payment.

Should an open dispute be shown as money already recovered?

Use confirmed movements in the reconciliation. Show the open status and potential recovery separately. The appropriate reviewer determines how the circumstances affect the accounting presentation.

What if the deduction is hidden inside a later payout?

Obtain the transaction-level provider statement and connect its adjustments to the combined settlement. The bank record should match the actual net movement; the supporting schedule explains its components.

Can a manager use one case list for several villas?

Yes, provided every case identifies the correct property, entity, booking, payment and responsible person. A combined list should still allow a separate owner statement to be prepared for each property.
